questions.question: What does [x * x | x <- [1,2,3]] evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The output function x * x is applied to each drawn value: 1*1=1, 2*2=4, 3*3=9, giving [1,4,9]. The generator supplies the inputs; the output function decides what goes into the result.
optionFeedback: This is what [x | x <- [1,2,3]] gives — the output function here is x * x, not just x.
Correct — each x is squared before being collected: 1, 4, 9.
This would be the output for [x * 2 | x <- [1,2,3]] — doubling, not squaring.
The comprehension produces one output value per input value, not the input list repeated.

questions.question: In [(x, x * 2) | x <- [1,2,3]], what is the output function?
options: (x, x * 2) — everything before the pipe, which happens to build a tuple
There is no output function in this comprehension
questions.explanation: The output function is whatever appears before the pipe, in full — here that is the tuple expression (x, x * 2), not just one piece of it. It is evaluated once per value x takes, producing a tuple each time.
optionFeedback: That's the generator, which lives after the pipe and supplies the values of x.
x * 2 is only half of the output expression — the output function here builds a whole tuple, (x, x * 2).
Correct — the output function is everything before the pipe, and it can be any expression, including one that builds a tuple.
Every comprehension has an output function — it's mandatory, and it's the part before the pipe.

questions.question: What does [x | x <- [1..10], mod x 2 == 0] evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The generator draws x from 1 to 10; the test mod x 2 == 0 keeps only the values divisible by 2 with no remainder. That keeps 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and drops the odd values.
optionFeedback: These are the odd values — exactly what this test excludes, since mod x 2 == 0 keeps evens, not odds.
Correct — every even value from 1 to 10, in order.
This is the ungenerated, unfiltered range — the test mod x 2 == 0 removes the odd values from it.
0 never appears in the generator's range [1..10] at all, and even if it did, the output function here is just x, not a computed remainder.

questions.question: What does [x | x <- [1..50], mod x 3 == 0, mod x 5 == 0] keep?
options: Multiples of 3 or multiples of 5
Multiples of both 3 and 5 — i.e. multiples of 15
Numbers that are multiples of neither 3 nor 5
Every number from 1 to 50, since the two tests cancel out
questions.explanation: Comma-separated tests are all required — this is an AND, not an OR. A value passes only if it satisfies mod x 3 == 0 AND mod x 5 == 0, which means it's a multiple of both 3 and 5, i.e. a multiple of 15: 15, 30, 45.
optionFeedback: Comma-separated tests require ALL of them to hold — this would be the result of an OR, which commas don't express.
Correct — every listed test must hold simultaneously, which narrows the result down to multiples of 15.
This describes values failing both tests — the opposite of what the comprehension keeps.
The tests don't cancel out; they combine with AND, narrowing the result rather than leaving it unfiltered.

questions.question: [x + y | x <- [1,2,3], y <- [-3,0,3]] produces nine results. Which generator varies fastest, and what does that mean concretely?
options: The leftmost generator (x) varies fastest — x runs through all three of its values while y stays fixed at -3
The rightmost generator (y) varies fastest — x is held at 1 while y runs through all three of its values, then x becomes 2 and y runs through all three again, and so on
Both generators vary at the same rate, in lockstep
Neither generator "varies faster" than the other — the nine results appear in an arbitrary order
questions.explanation: The lesson states this directly: the rightmost generator varies fastest, exactly like the innermost loop of a nested loop. x is fixed at 1 while y takes -3, 0, then 3 (three results), then x becomes 2 and y cycles through all three again, and so on for x = 3 — nine results total, in a fixed, predictable order.
optionFeedback: It's the other way around — the RIGHTMOST generator (y here) is the one that cycles through all its values first, for each fixed value of the leftmost one.
Correct — y is the rightmost generator and cycles fastest, exactly as a nested loop with y innermost would.
The two generators do not advance together; one is held fixed while the other cycles through its entire range before the first one advances.
The order is fixed and predictable, not arbitrary — it is exactly the order a nested loop with y innermost would produce, which is precisely why the rightmost-varies-fastest rule is worth memorising.

questions.question: In [(x, y) | x <- [1..4], y <- [x..4]], the later generator y <- [x..4] refers to x, the earlier generator's variable. What does this dependency accomplish?
options: It is a syntax error — a later generator can never refer to an earlier one
It restricts y's range based on the current value of x, so pairs like (2,1) — where y is smaller than x — are never generated in the first place, rather than being generated and then filtered out
It makes x and y always equal to each other
It has no effect; y <- [x..4] behaves identically to y <- [1..4]
questions.explanation: A later generator is allowed to use any name already bound by an earlier one. Here, once x is fixed (say, at 2), y <- [x..4] draws only from [2..4], so (2,1) is never produced — the comprehension avoids generating a combination it would only have to discard with a separate test.
optionFeedback: This is valid, working Haskell — the transcript directly above shows its actual output, produced without any error.
Correct — the dependency narrows y's starting point to the current x, producing only pairs where y >= x, with no separate filtering test needed.
The output [(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,2),...] includes many pairs where x and y differ, e.g. (1,4) — they are not forced to be equal.
[x..4] and [1..4] are different ranges whenever x is greater than 1 — for x = 3, [x..4] is [3,4], not [1,2,3,4].

check-comprehensions-over-tuples-and-str.title: Check: comprehensions over tuples and strings

questions.question: In [name | (name, mark) <- marks, mark >= 70], what is (name, mark) doing as the generator's left-hand side?
options: It is a tuple pattern that destructures each pair in marks as it is drawn, binding name and mark separately, in the same step
It builds a new tuple from the elements of marks, doubling their size
It is invalid syntax; generators may only bind a single plain variable
It filters marks down to only the pairs, discarding anything that isn't a pair
questions.explanation: A generator's left-hand side can be any pattern, not just a bare name. (name, mark) <- marks matches each element of marks — already a (String, Integer) pair — and binds name and mark to its two components in one step, exactly the way a where clause's tuple pattern would.
optionFeedback: Correct — this is a tuple pattern used as a generator, destructuring while generating, exactly as this section's opening sentence describes.
Nothing is built or resized here; the pattern only takes apart pairs that already exist in marks, it does not construct new ones.
Generators accept any pattern on their left, tuple patterns included — this is exactly what makes list-of-tuple data usable directly inside a comprehension.
marks is already entirely pairs by construction ([(String, Integer)]); there is nothing here to filter out — every element matches (name, mark).

questions.question: The lesson runs [name | (name, mark) <- marks, mark >= 70] and [name | (name, mark) <- marks, mark < 70] side by side and calls the results "complementary". What does that mean here?
options: The two results are identical lists
Between the two lists, every student in marks is accounted for exactly once — the two tests partition marks into two disjoint groups with no overlap and no one left out
The second list is always empty because the first test already used every mark
The two comprehensions use different generators, not just different tests
questions.explanation: mark >= 70 and mark < 70 are exact opposites for any Integer — every mark satisfies exactly one of them, never both and never neither. So running the same generator with both tests splits marks into two lists that, put together, contain every original student exactly once.
optionFeedback: The two results are actually shown to be different in the lesson's exact output: ["Kago","Thato"] versus ["Naledi"] — not identical.
Correct — every student satisfies exactly one of mark >= 70 or mark < 70, so the two lists between them cover marks completely with no overlap.

The second list, for this data, has one student (Naledi) — it is not empty, and there is no mechanism by which one comprehension's test would empty out a separate, independently-evaluated comprehension.
Both comprehensions use the exact same generator, (name, mark) <- marks — only the trailing test differs between them.

questions.question: A student predicts that the first line of output below will be [(1,'a'),(2,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'b')], because "the first generator should run fastest". The second line puzzles them as well, since it produces only two pairs. Which explanation covers both results?
options: The first line prints the student's prediction, and the second prints every pair from 1 to 4.

The first line prints [(1,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'a'),(2,'b')] and the second prints [(1,4),(2,3)]. The rightmost generator varies fastest, like the innermost loop of nested loops: x stays at 1 while y runs through 'a' and 'b', then x moves to 2. In the second line the generator y <- [x .. 4] depends on x, so only pairs with y at least x are produced, and the test x + y == 5 keeps just the two whose sum is five.
The first line prints [(1,'a'),(2,'b')], because generators are paired up element by element like zip.
The first line is a type error, because x and y have different types, and the second line prints nothing.
questions.explanation: Multiple generators describe a nested loop with the last one innermost. A later generator may use an earlier one, which avoids producing combinations that would be thrown away, and tests filter the combinations that remain.
optionFeedback: The order is wrong, and the second line has a test that removes most pairs. The rightmost generator varies fastest.
Correct. The ordering rule and the dependent generator together explain both results.
Generators combine every element of one list with every element of the other; they are not paired element by element.
x and y may have different types in a comprehension. The first line is valid, and the second prints two pairs.

questions.question: A lecturer shows the recursive and the comprehension versions below and asks which is "better". A student says: "The comprehension is always the right choice and recursion is obsolete." Which response best describes how the two forms relate and when each is needed?
options: The student is right, because a comprehension can express every list function, including ones that compare neighbouring elements such as isSorted.

The two functions produce the same list. The comprehension states what the result is (each x from xs that is positive), while the recursion states how to build it step by step. The comprehension is clearer when the result is each element of a list, transformed or filtered, but recursion is needed when the answer depends on more than one element at a time, for example checking whether neighbours are in order.
The recursive version is better because it is faster, since comprehensions need to build an intermediate list first.
The two functions produce different results for negative numbers, because a comprehension always keeps them.
questions.explanation: A comprehension is declarative: it describes a list in terms of another list. Recursion is the more general mechanism and is the right tool when the structure of the computation does not fit one-element-at-a-time transformation or filtering.
optionFeedback: Comprehensions process elements independently. A property such as being sorted depends on how neighbouring elements relate, which needs recursion or a different tool.
Correct. The forms are interchangeable for filters and maps, and recursion remains necessary for problems that look at several elements together.
No performance claim is made, and neither form is automatically faster. The choice here is about clarity and what the problem needs.
Both functions drop the elements that are not positive. The test x > 0 removes the negative ones in the comprehension.

questions.question: A student reads the last line of the program below and predicts [2,4], because "the output only mentions x and y does nothing". Which explanation of the actual output is correct?
options: The first line prints [2,4]; the other two are errors, because comma-separated tests and && cannot both be valid.

The first line prints [2,2,4,4]. The generator y <- [1 .. 2] runs for every x that survives the test, so each surviving x is produced once per y, even though the output expression never mentions y. The last two lines both print [15,30,45], because commas between tests mean and, and joining the conditions with && inside a single test is equivalent.
The first line prints [1,2,3,4,5], because a test placed before a generator is ignored.
The first line prints [(2,1),(2,2),(4,1),(4,2)], because the output is always built from all the variables.
questions.explanation: A generator multiplies the number of results even when its variable is not used in the output. Tests are applied at the point where they appear, so the test even x filters x before y is generated. The two ways of writing a conjunction of conditions are equivalent.
optionFeedback: Both styles are valid and give the same result. The first line is not [2,4] either, because y is generated for each surviving x.
Correct. The unused variable still produces duplicates, which is a common surprise, and the two forms of combining tests agree.
A test is not ignored; it filters the elements generated so far, so the odd values are removed.
The output expression is x, so only x appears in each result. y affects only how many times each x is produced.
